idiom_name: central decision point behind a container interceptor, with the principal transported by Subject.doAs
implementation_notes: Java's historic mediation mechanism was the JVM itself: AccessController.checkPermission walked the call stack and threw unless every caller's protection domain held the permission, with doPrivileged marking the caller at which checking stopped. That mechanism is deprecated for removal (JEP 411) and permanently disabled in later releases (JEP 486), and it has no replacement, so new code must not be built on it. What replaces the classic structure is a framework or container enforcement point - a servlet filter, a CDI/EJB method-permission interceptor or an explicit mediator service - that runs the check for every operation, with the authenticated principal carried across API and thread boundaries by Subject.doAs (and the subject accessor that replaces the SecurityManager-dependent getSubject). A mediator class that wraps the resource and checks in every method is the portable form and the only option when access does not come through a container request.
pitfalls: doPrivileged (and any equivalent privileged-caller marker) widens rights for the whole call stack below it; the deprecated JVM mechanism shows the failure mode - a wide privileged block defeats the purpose, and the API is being removed.

Principal propagation is manual on threads: a Subject bound to a request thread is lost in thread pools and asynchronous stages unless it is re-bound with Subject.doAs, and the worker then runs unmediated with no identity.
Thread-pool reuse leaks the previous request's principal unless the binding is cleared (finally, or the framework's clear hook); a stale subject passes the mediator as someone else.
Caching AccessControlContext or authorization decisions in a static map outlives revocation - nothing in the JVM invalidates it for you.
